summary: Location servers that hold emergency routing information can return it along with location when asked. This standards-track RFC extends the HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery (HELD) protocol to request routing information in the same request as location, and updates RFC 5985.

eli5.summary: Asking where you are and who to call in an emergency in one question instead of two.

questions: what is held routing request extension
how do emergency calls get routed with held
subtitle: Lets a device ask a location server for emergency call routing in the same request that asks for its location.

tldr.problem: Emergency call routing normally needs a separate LoST lookup after location is obtained, but many regions have not deployed LoST servers or forest guides.
tldr.mechanism: A new requestRoutingInformation element in a HELD locationRequest asks the location server (LIS) to also return a routingInformation element holding PSAP or gateway URIs for the device's location.
tldr.outcome: Location and routing arrive in one exchange, and the RFC updates RFC 5985 and RFC 6881 so that HELD clients always ask for routing information.

today: RFC 7840 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5985 and RFC 6881, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The emergency calling models in RFC 6443 and RFC 6881 expect a local LoST (Location-to-Service Translation) server, or a network of forest guides, to find the PSAP (Public Safety Answering Point) best placed to handle a call. The RFC notes that networks of forest guides have not materialized and that LoST deployment is not ubiquitous. Some regions and countries have expressed reluctance to deploy LoST servers.

This document extends the HELD protocol (RFC 5985) so that a location information server can provide emergency routing information when no LoST server or forest-guide network exists. It is aimed at architectures, such as those behind regulatory requirements in Europe, that couple location and routing in the access network.
sections.eli5: Normally you ask one office where you are and a second office who to call. Some places do not have the second office, so this lets the first office answer both.

sections.title: Why Routing Comes From the LIS
sections.content:
RFC 6881 describes two calling models. In the device-centric model the phone gets its location with HELD and then asks LoST for the next hop toward the local PSAP. In the softswitch-centric model the serving softswitch notices an emergency call, fetches the caller's location from the LIS, and then asks LoST for the route.

LoST servers are geographically bound, while a LIS is bound to a domain. When a domain spans several regions, the LoST server found may not be able to route to the right PSAP and needs forest guides, and the RFC says no public forest guides have been deployed in the countries it discusses. Meanwhile the LIS often already knows the PSAP URI: it may validate civic locations using LoST, learn the PSAP at provisioning time, or always route to the same emergency provider.

The authors also considered reusing the LoST mapping element. They rejected that because its mandatory source attribute would be misleading when there is no authoritative LoST server, and expiry details are irrelevant because the routing data must not be cached.
sections.eli5: The office that knows where you are often already knows the right emergency centre too. Making you visit a second office that may not exist is a waste.

sections.title: The Request and Response Mechanism
sections.content:
The mechanism adds one element to the HELD locationRequest and one to the locationResponse. The request element, requestRoutingInformation, says the requestor wants routing information based on the end device's location. With no attribute, URIs for urn:service:sos are returned. The requestor may add an optional service URN, which MUST exist in the IANA Service URN Labels repository. If the LIS does not understand the requested service, it returns urn:service:sos URIs.

If the LIS has routing information, it returns a routingInformation element in the response. How the LIS obtains it is left to the implementation. A LIS that does not understand the request element ignores it and returns location normally. A LIS that supports it MUST support urn:service:sos and regionally defined sub-services, and MUST return correct routing information if it has or can acquire it.

If the LIS understands the request but cannot find routing information for the location, it MUST set the defaultRoute attribute to true and return a default PSAP or gateway URI together with the location. The response holds a service element named by a service URN, with one or more dest URIs, each URI scheme appearing only once. Routing URIs are meant for use when received and MUST NOT be cached.
sections.eli5: You tick a box saying you also want to know who to call. If the office has an answer it writes it down, and if it only has a general answer it marks it as a fallback.

sections.title: Changes to the Emergency Calling BCP
sections.content:
This document updates the Phone BCP, RFC 6881. Devices and intermediaries that use HELD must always include the routing extension. If the LIS is configured with routing information it supplies it; otherwise the device or intermediary tries LoST to get the PSAP URI.

  • Requirement ED-23/INT-18/SP-14 is updated so that, when HELD is the location configuration protocol, the request MUST include the requestRoutingInformation element.
  • New ED-51a: endpoints MUST support the element and be able to use any routing information returned.
  • New ED-52a: endpoints that get routing information SHOULD use it but MAY still perform a LoST findService request if they have a location value.
  • New ED-52b: if the response has defaultRoute set to true, endpoints with a location value MUST perform a LoST findService request. A route from LoST MUST be used; otherwise the HELD routing information SHOULD be used.

SP-26 is also amended so a LoST mapping need not be requested when non-default routing information is provided.
sections.eli5: The rulebook now says: always ask for the who-to-call answer along with where-you-are. If the answer is only a fallback, double-check with the second office when you can.

sections.title: The Schema Extension
sections.content:
Section 6 of the RFC gives an XML schema in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:geopriv:held:ri. It defines three pieces.

  • requestRoutingInformation: an empty element with an optional service attribute, defaulting to urn:service:sos.
  • routingInformation: holds one service element, plus optional elements from other namespaces.
  • service: one or more dest URIs, an optional defaultRoute boolean that defaults to false, and a required serviceUri attribute.

IANA has registered the namespace and the schema, using the guidelines of RFC 3688. The schema XML is the whole of section 6 of the RFC.
sections.eli5: The RFC adds two new boxes to the form: one to ask for the answer and one to hold it. The answer box lists the phone addresses to try.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives three examples. The first is a locationRequest with responseTime set to emergencyRouting, a requestRoutingInformation element and IP flow information.

The second is a locationResponse with two location URIs (one HTTPS, one SIP) plus a routingInformation element for urn:service:sos listing sip:, sips: and xmpp: destinations. The third is similar, with one HTTPS location URI and defaultRoute set to true on the service.
sections.eli5: The examples show a filled-in form asking the question, and two filled-in answers: one normal, one marked as a fallback.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it makes no changes needing privacy considerations beyond those in RFC 5985, though it does extend those in RFC 6155. RFC 6155 lets authorized third parties acquire location from a LIS. Because the routing extension returns URIs for services near the target, it reveals extra information about the target. The RFC therefore recommends using this option only when the LIS returns a location URI, not a location value.

On security, the document adds no considerations beyond those already in RFC 5985 and RFC 6155.
sections.eli5: Knowing which emergency centre is near you tells people a little about where you are. So the RFC suggests handing out a pointer to your location instead of the location itself.
